pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Chromosomes, Genes & DNA

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 biology — 'heredity as the process by which genetic information is transmitted from one generation to the next; a simple model of chromosomes, genes and DNA in heredity, including the part played by Watson, Crick, Franklin and Wilkins'):** The KS3 programme names this hierarchy AND the historical scientists explicitly — both the model and the story of its discovery are required.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-LS3-1 / MS-LS3-2):** Genes are located on chromosomes; each gene carries instructions affecting traits; [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS3-2] — the structural picture (DNA→gene→chromosome) grounds these heredity ideas.

- **Operational details:** Build the nested hierarchy explicitly and in scale order: cell → nucleus → chromosome → (unravels into) one long DNA molecule → a gene is a SECTION of that DNA. Establish the key facts: DNA is a double helix (two strands, base pairs); a gene is a length of DNA that codes for a characteristic (a protein); human body cells have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Confront the two hardest ideas for this age: (a) scale — a single chromosome is ONE immensely long, tightly coiled DNA molecule, not a bag of separate DNA bits; (b) part-whole — a gene is not separate FROM DNA, it IS a stretch of DNA. Teach the discovery as real collaborative and contested science: Franklin's and Wilkins's X-ray crystallography (Photo 51) provided the evidence Watson and Crick used to build the double-helix model — a chance to discuss evidence, credit and the nature of science.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/abstract). Success means holding an invisible, multi-level nested model in mind and reasoning about part-whole and scale relationships: order the DNA→gene→chromosome→nucleus→cell hierarchy, say what a gene codes for, state 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, and describe the four scientists' contributions.
bestPractices: Teach the hierarchy as a literal zoom through nested scales (cell→nucleus→chromosome→DNA→gene) so the part-whole relationships are concrete, not a list of words.
Make explicit that one chromosome IS a single very long, coiled DNA molecule — the commonest structural confusion at this level.
Define a gene as a SECTION of DNA that codes for a characteristic, so students see genes as parts of DNA rather than separate objects.
Use the discovery story (Franklin/Wilkins X-ray data → Watson–Crick model) to teach nature-of-science ideas: evidence, model-building, collaboration and the debate over credit to Rosalind Franklin.
Anchor abstract structure with physical/analogical models (a coiled rope for chromosome→DNA, a twisted ladder for the helix) while flagging the limits of each analogy.
Give concrete numbers (46 chromosomes, 23 pairs) and a concrete gene example (a gene 'for' a characteristic) to keep the abstraction tethered.
keyRepresentations: A zoom/drill-down sequence: cell → nucleus → chromosome → unravelled DNA → highlighted gene, each level nested inside the last.
The double-helix 'twisted ladder' model with base pairs as rungs.
A coiled-rope analogy showing a chromosome as one long DNA molecule wound up tightly.
A karyotype image showing 23 pairs of human chromosomes.
Franklin's X-ray diffraction 'Photo 51' alongside the Watson–Crick model, illustrating evidence → model.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a chromosome contains many separate pieces of DNA, rather than being ONE long coiled DNA molecule.
Treating genes, DNA and chromosomes as three separate kinds of thing rather than nested parts of one structure (gene = section of DNA; DNA coils into a chromosome).
Believing DNA/genes are only in special cells (e.g. sex cells or blood) rather than in the nucleus of nearly every body cell.
Confusing a gene (a section of DNA coding for a characteristic) with a whole chromosome, or with a single 'trait' with no physical basis.
Assuming Watson and Crick discovered DNA's structure alone, unaware that Franklin's and Wilkins's X-ray evidence was essential.
Muddling the numbers — e.g. thinking humans have 23 chromosomes rather than 46 (23 pairs).

learn.summary: For ages 12–13: build an explicit, nested-scale model of DNA, genes and chromosomes (cell → nucleus → chromosome → one long DNA molecule → a gene as a section of that DNA), fix the key facts (double helix with base pairs; 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs; a gene codes for a protein, which in turn affects a characteristic), and teach the contested discovery story (X-ray crystallography at King's College London by Franklin and by Wilkins; Photo 51 was taken in Franklin's lab by Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling, and Wilkins showed it to Watson without Franklin's knowledge; this evidence helped Watson and Crick build the double-helix model). The core learning objective is holding this multi-level structure in mind and reasoning about part-whole and scale relationships, plus discussing evidence, credit and the nature of science.

activities.title: Zoom down the scales: from cell to a single gene
feedback: If a learner says a chromosome 'contains many separate bits of DNA', return to the unwinding step: one uncopied chromosome unspools into a single continuous DNA thread — it is one molecule wound up tight (an X-shaped, copied chromosome is just two identical such threads joined together).

If a learner treats gene, DNA and chromosome as three separate kinds of object, point back to the highlighted stretch: the gene lit up is part of the same DNA strand, and that strand coils up to form the chromosome.
If a learner orders the levels wrongly (e.g. genes as the biggest), rebuild from base: DNA base → gene (a short section) → DNA molecule → chromosome (coiled DNA) → nucleus → cell.
If a learner thinks DNA is only in special cells (sex cells, blood), note that this nucleus-and-DNA picture is true of nearly every body cell.
activities.rationale: Walking down the nested scales one level at a time makes the part-whole relationships concrete rather than a list of words, and the unwinding step targets the commonest structural confusion directly. An interactive drill-down where tapping an element zooms into a child illustration maps closely onto this hierarchy; a careful labelled drawing, printed zoom sequence or animation can serve the same purpose with the unwinding shown explicitly. The highlight/zoom and fact-cards are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not required technology.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 biology requires a simple model of chromosomes, genes and DNA in heredity, including the part played by Watson, Crick, Franklin and Wilkins.

NGSS MS-LS3-1 places mutations 'located on chromosomes' affecting proteins and traits (genes reside on chromosomes and carry instructions affecting traits), and MS-LS3-2 establishes that [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-LS3-2] while asexual reproduction yields identical genetic information.
learnerActions: Start from a single body cell and work inwards one level at a time: cell → nucleus → chromosome → DNA molecule → gene.

At the chromosome level, watch (or trace, in a drawn/animated version) a single chromosome unwind into one single, very long twisted-ladder DNA molecule. (The familiar X shape is a chromosome that has been copied before the cell divides: two identical DNA molecules joined together, so each arm of the X unwinds into its own DNA molecule.)
Along the unwound helix, identify and highlight a short stretch and label it: 'a gene — a section of DNA that codes for a protein (which in turn affects a characteristic).'
Record the key numbers at the right level: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs in a human body cell; the double helix has two strands with base pairs as rungs.
Cross-link the helix view to a karyotype image showing the 23 pairs.
activities.intendedInsight: A chromosome is not a bag of separate DNA pieces — an uncopied chromosome IS one enormously long, tightly coiled DNA molecule (the X shape seen before division is two identical copies joined together); and a gene is not separate from DNA but a stretch OF it. The levels nest inside one another in scale order.

activities.title: Handle the double helix in three dimensions
feedback: If a learner reads the helix as a flat ladder, have them rotate the model to see the twist and the two strands winding around each other in the same twisting direction, joined by the rungs.
If a learner expects biochemistry detail on the bases, keep it at model level: the rungs pair up in a fixed way; naming specific bases is beyond this stage.
If the coiling seems implausible, demonstrate with a long rope or thread wound tightly to show length versus packed size.
activities.rationale: A manipulable 3D or physical helix adds spatial understanding of the twist and base-pairing that a single flat diagram shows less vividly, and unwinding a 3D/physical chromosome makes coiling tangible. This illuminates one spatial part of the topic; the assessable core (hierarchy, facts, history) is mostly non-spatial, so this complements rather than replaces the zoom activity. A physical card/rope model has real thickness and can be handled; treat it as an approximation of the idealised molecule.
learnerActions: Rotate and inspect a double helix (physical model, 3D on-screen model, or built twisted-ladder) to see the two strands twisting around each other with base pairs as rungs.
Unspool a 3D or physical chromosome model into its DNA thread to feel how a huge length coils into a compact structure.
Point out complementary base pairs at model level (rungs pair up) without going into GCSE-level biochemistry.
Zoom in on one gene segment and relate it back to the whole helix.
activities.intendedInsight: The helix is genuinely three-dimensional — two strands, base pairs, a twist — and extreme coiling is how a very long molecule fits inside a tiny nucleus.

activities.title: Talk to Rosalind Franklin about Photo 51
feedback: If a learner assumes Watson and Crick worked alone, return to the evidence chain: the X-ray diffraction data came first and the model was built using it.
If a learner can name the scientists but not their roles, separate evidence-gatherers (Franklin, Wilkins) from model-builders (Watson, Crick) and have them restate who did what.
Encourage reasoned opinions on the credit question rather than a single 'right' verdict.
activities.rationale: Discussing the discovery in role turns nature-of-science ideas into a vivid, personal exchange and directly meets the curriculum requirement to cover the scientists' parts. An open conversation builds the history and nature-of-science strand well but will not reliably build the structural hierarchy, so it should accompany the visual/zoom model rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: Rosalind Franklin's and Maurice Wilkins's X-ray diffraction data (notably 'Photo 51') provided key evidence that Watson and Crick used to build the double-helix model of DNA.
DfE KS3 biology requires a simple model of chromosomes, genes and DNA in heredity, including the part played by Watson, Crick, Franklin and Wilkins.
learnerActions: Interview (in role-play, or with a prepared in-role script) Rosalind Franklin or Maurice Wilkins about what X-ray crystallography is and what Photo 51 showed.
Ask how that evidence fed into the model Watson and Crick built.
Probe the fairness of credit: who provided the evidence, who built the model, and how recognition was shared.
Summarise each of the four scientists' contributions in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: DNA's structure was discovered through real collaborative and contested science: X-ray evidence from King's College London (Wilkins's work, and Franklin's, including Photo 51, taken by Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling and shown to Watson by Wilkins without her knowledge) provided key evidence for the Watson–Crick model, raising genuine questions about evidence, credit and how science works.

activities.title: Build and consolidate the hierarchy
feedback: If the nesting is reversed, rebuild from the gene outward: gene (section of DNA) → DNA molecule → coiled chromosome → nucleus → cell.
If the number is given as 23 chromosomes, clarify: 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs.

If a learner defines a gene as the trait itself or a tiny picture of a body part, correct to: a gene is an instruction that codes for a protein, and proteins build and run the body — that is how genes affect characteristics.
If the 'chromosome = many DNA pieces' idea reappears, link back to the unwinding activity.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, matching, nesting and recall consolidate the model and let specific misconceptions (chromosome as many pieces; genes only in special cells; reversed hierarchy) be surfaced and addressed. These tasks mainly check and reinforce recall; on their own they confirm rather than build the nested mental model, so they follow the zoom and manipulation activities. The drag-and-nest builder with feedback is an optional interaction example.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 biology requires a simple model of chromosomes, genes and DNA in heredity, including the part played by Watson, Crick, Franklin and Wilkins.
learnerActions: Assemble the hierarchy by nesting: place a gene inside a DNA molecule, inside a chromosome, inside the nucleus, inside the cell — in correct scale order (drag-and-nest, cut-out cards, or a drawn diagram).
Order the five levels from smallest to largest: DNA base, gene, chromosome, nucleus, cell.
Match each scientist (Watson, Crick, Franklin, Wilkins) to their contribution.
Fill in the numbers: human body cells have ___ chromosomes in ___ pairs (46; 23).
State in a sentence what a gene is and what it codes for.
Answer a check question such as: does a chromosome contain many separate DNA pieces, or is it one long coiled DNA molecule?
activities.intendedInsight: The facts, numbers, part-whole nesting and discovery roles can be stated accurately and in the correct order.

activities.title: Why do identical-DNA cells differ? (differential expression)
feedback: Full understanding: rejects the claim, explains all body cells share the same genome but express different genes, nests DNA–gene–chromosome–nucleus–cell correctly, and says a gene codes for a protein.
Partial: knows cells share the same DNA OR can state the hierarchy, but lists terms without linking them — prompt them to say what a gene codes for and why identical DNA can yield different cells.

Gap/misconception ('each cell holds only its own genes'): establish genome constancy — body cells all came from the same fertilised egg by division, and nearly every body cell carries the same full DNA (exceptions include mature red blood cells, which have no nucleus); differences come from which genes are switched on.
activities.rationale: This claim cleanly splits learners who hold the genome-in-every-cell idea from those with the common 'each cell has only its own genes' misconception (documented by Lewis & Wood-Robinson in the source row's assessment notes), and the follow-up reveals whether the DNA–gene–chromosome hierarchy is secure. Expressed-not-held is the key corrective idea.
learnerActions: Consider the claim: 'A skin cell contains the genes for skin, and a muscle cell contains the genes for muscle — that's why they differ.' Decide whether it is right and explain.
Explain what each cell actually contains in terms of DNA, genes and chromosomes.
Answer the probe: if every body cell has the same DNA, why doesn't a muscle cell look and behave like a skin cell?
State what a gene codes for and how that links to cell differences.
activities.intendedInsight: Nearly every body cell carries the SAME complete genome (all 46 chromosomes, all the genes); cell types differ because they USE (express) different genes, not because they hold different genes.

constraints: Target age 12–13; keep base-pairing at model level (rungs pair up) and avoid GCSE-level biochemistry and unexplained technical terms.
Recall/matching/sequencing tasks confirm and reinforce the facts but do not by themselves build the nested mental model — pair them with the zoom and manipulation work.
An open in-role conversation develops the history and nature-of-science strand but will not reliably establish the structural hierarchy; use it alongside the visual model.
Physical and card/rope models have real thickness and are approximations of the idealised molecule; name any zero-thickness on-screen version as a model.
Flag the limits of each analogy explicitly: a coiled rope stands for chromosome-as-coiled-DNA, a twisted ladder for the helix — neither is the thing itself.
State clearly that a gene codes for a protein, and proteins in turn affect characteristics; do not teach a gene as being, or being a miniature picture of, the characteristic itself.
The credit/fairness question is for reasoned discussion, not a single scripted 'correct' answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source row marks the UK DfE and NGSS curriculum claims as verified and the Franklin/Wilkins Photo 51 historical claim as not verified (verified:false); the historical-evidence claim is presented as 'key evidence' (matching the source's own wording and the row's 'crucial' framing) with the credit debate handled as discussion rather than settled adjudication.

The source row phrases a gene as coding 'for a characteristic (a protein)', treating characteristic and protein as equivalent; corrected in the learner-facing guidance to gene → protein → characteristic, consistent with the row's own error-pattern remediation.

The 'Lewis & Wood-Robinson' attribution for the 'each cell has only its own genes' misconception comes from the row's assessment field and is not backed by a listed source entry; retained as the row's stated basis, not independently confirmed here.
The source row's domain tag ('Ecosystems & Habitats') does not match the genetics topic; likely a mislabel, noted but not altered.

The NGSS source claim is reproduced verbatim (including its muddled 'mutations located on chromosomes' phrasing) only as a justification reference; this wording is not repeated in any learner-facing text.

Original 'ideal/strong/possible' catalog fit rankings and claims that certain insights can be delivered 'rather than by being told' or that 'no diagram can' match a conversation were softened to scoped affordances; comparative efficacy is not established by the available sources.

In an independent re-audit, the term 'antiparallel strands' in the 3D-helix feedback was simplified to 'two strands running in opposite directions' to match the stated age level and avoid GCSE-level jargon.

probeDeeper: If every body cell has the same DNA, why doesn't a muscle cell look and behave like a skin cell?
Put these in order from smallest to largest: gene, chromosome, DNA base, nucleus, cell.
Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photograph was crucial — what did it show, and what did Watson and Crick do with it?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Nearly every body cell contains the SAME complete set of DNA — all 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), all the genes. Skin and muscle cells differ because they USE (express) different genes, not because they hold different ones. The hierarchy: DNA coils up into chromosomes inside the nucleus of the cell, and a gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein.

errorPatterns.pattern: Different cell types contain different genes/DNA — 'skin cells carry skin genes, muscle cells carry muscle genes'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish genome constancy: every body cell came from the same fertilised egg by division and carries the same full DNA; differences come from which genes are switched on.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — skin cells carry the skin genes and muscle cells carry the muscle genes, which is why they differ.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees the cells differ because they hold different genes, rather than because they express different ones

errorPatterns.pattern: Hierarchy/scale reversed — 'genes are the biggest; chromosomes and DNA fit inside genes'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the nesting concretely: a chromosome is one long coiled DNA molecule; a gene is a short section of that DNA; order from base to cell.
errorPatterns.distractor: Genes are the biggest — chromosomes and DNA fit inside the genes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Nests the levels the wrong way when asked to order them

errorPatterns.pattern: Gene as a blueprint-picture — 'a gene is a tiny version of the feature it makes'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Replace the picture with the code idea: a gene is an instruction that codes for a protein; proteins build and run the body, which is how genes affect features.
errorPatterns.distractor: A gene is a tiny blueprint-picture of the feature it produces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a gene AS the trait or a miniature of the body part, not as coding for a protein

responseLevels.gap: Agrees each cell holds only its own genes; cannot order the hierarchy or reverses it (genes contain chromosomes).
responseLevels.full: Rejects the claim and explains all body cells hold the same genome but express different genes, correctly nests DNA-gene-chromosome-nucleus-cell, states a gene codes for a protein, and attributes the double-helix discovery roles.
responseLevels.partial: Knows all cells share the same DNA OR can state the hierarchy, but lists the terms without linking them — can't say a gene codes for a protein, or why identical DNA yields different cells; recites the discoverers' names without the differential-expression idea.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A student says: 'A skin cell contains the genes for skin, and a muscle cell contains the genes for muscle — that's why they turn out different.' Is that right? Explain what each of these cells actually contains, in terms of DNA, genes and chromosomes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the genome-in-every-cell idea rejects the claim and explains the difference by which genes are used. A child with the common 'each cell has only its own genes' idea (Lewis & Wood-Robinson) agrees with the statement — a clean split — and the follow-up exposes whether they can order the DNA-gene-chromosome hierarchy.
